title: How GPS knows where you are

audience.who: Corporate employees across functions, most of whom use phone navigation daily
audience.knows: That their phone shows a blue dot on a map and that satellites are involved somewhere; not how a position is actually worked out
audience.cares_about: Understanding an everyday tool they rely on, in a few minutes, without maths homework; a satisfying 'so that is how it works' they can repeat to a colleague

outcome: After watching, the viewer can explain in their own words how a phone turns satellite signals into a position: timed broadcasts, distance from travel time, intersecting spheres, a fourth satellite to fix the phone's clock, and why the satellites' clocks must be corrected for relativity.
through_line: GPS is a timing system: every step of finding where you are comes down to measuring time very precisely, and every correction exists to keep that time honest.

arc_plan.what: The moment the viewer meets the thing: you open a map and the blue dot appears; the phone sends nothing up, so how does it know? Pose the question of what happens in between.
A set of satellites on their orbits around Earth, each one continuously broadcasting where it is and the exact time by its onboard clock; the phone only listens.
arc_plan.source_anchor: from_user: request notes (satellite broadcast content to be grounded by the knowledge sheet)

arc_plan.what: The mechanism shown running: the signal travels to the phone, travel time times the speed of light gives distance, one distance is a sphere, two intersect in a circle, three narrow to points, a fourth satellite solves for the phone's cheap clock error and pins one point.

Why the timing must be so exact: a tiny clock error becomes a large distance error; the satellites' own clocks tick at a different rate in orbit because of their speed and weaker gravity, and without the built-in correction positions would drift.
arc_plan.source_anchor: from_user: request notes (rates and drift figures only as the knowledge sheet grounds them)

arc_plan.what: Return to the blue dot: it is the answer to a timing problem solved continuously; the through-line restated as the one idea to keep.

must_cover.what: Each satellite broadcasts its own position and the precise time of sending
The receiver (phone) only listens; it does not transmit to the satellites
Distance is computed from the signal's travel time at the speed of light
Spheres (circles in a 2D picture) of known distance intersect to narrow the position to one point
A fourth satellite is needed because the phone's clock is cheap and inaccurate; it solves for the clock error
Satellite clocks run at a different rate in orbit due to speed (special relativity) and weaker gravity (general relativity), and are corrected so positions do not drift
Why precision matters: a small timing error equals a large distance error at the speed of light

must_avoid: Invented numbers: no orbit heights, satellite counts, clock offsets or error distances unless the knowledge sheet grounds them
Claiming the phone sends anything up to the satellites
Vendor or product claims as fact (no phone brands, no app names)
Feature lists of GPS uses in place of the mechanism
Jargon before the picture (pseudorange, ephemeris, trilateration named before they are shown)
Popular myths stated as fact (for example that relativity correction is a single exact figure without a source)
example_posture: The everyday moment first: one person's phone in one city at night, finding itself; the same phone carries every step so the viewer follows one problem through. Hypothetical numbers only inside explicit framing ('say the signal took...'), real numbers only from the sheet.
visual_direction: A cosmic field at night: Earth, satellites on visible orbits, signals drawn as expanding wavefronts travelling to a single point on the ground. Distance shown as a growing sphere or circle; intersections building one at a time until one point lights. Clocks as instruments on the satellites and the phone, with their offset visible; the relativity part as two clocks side by side drifting apart, then corrected. One loud thing at a time; one diagram that builds and returns. A scale journey from orbit down to the phone and back fits.
voice_note: Mentor: a capable colleague walking you through something they find genuinely elegant, calm and precise. Curious, not breathless; it lets a picture land before the next line, and never talks down.
open_questions: Does the flat-cosmos style have a designed character kit? If not, the lesson uses no people (the phone alone carries the viewer), per the request.
Which real figures (orbit altitude, constellation size, clock rate offsets per day, drift per day) the knowledge sheet can ground; the script uses only those.
